reached.fact: A stranger with no credential is admitted as a peer. On the transports that prove no key — `tcp-testing-only` and the ACCEPTING side of `websocket` — `NetConn::verified_peer()` returns `None`, so the node admits a CapTP session from anyone who sends a single self-signed `op:start-session`: the peer signs the `my-location` payload with a key it generates itself, so the only check the node runs (`location_signature_is_valid`) proves possession of that fresh key and nothing about identity. Reachability: connect to the bound listener, send that one record. `session.verified_peer_key()` is the default `None` (`ocapn/src/netlayer.rs:64`, `ocapn/src/websocket.rs:494` with `verified = None` on accept per `ocapn/src/websocket.rs:410`), and the accept path checks only the self-signature (`ocapn/src/conn.rs:414`).

On the admitted session a stranger drives the node to act, and pay, as itself. The peer addresses the bootstrap at `<desc:export 0>` (inserted at position 0 by `ocapn/src/conn.rs:524`), `fetch`es the chain-backed capability under the guessable constant swiss number `rho:rchain:revVault/getBalance`, and a delivery to it is turned into a Rholang term, signed with the NODE's own deployer key (`signed_invoke`) and submitted to the block API (`block_api.deploy`), spending the node's REV and making the far contract see the node as caller. Reachability: `fetch` the constant swiss, then `op:deliver` to the returned capability. Bounded only by the node-wide `BRIDGED_DEPLOYMENTS_PER_SEC = 4` limiter and phlo, not by any per-peer bound. The capability is published on every session's bootstrap whenever a listener and a deployer key exist (`node/src/runtime/node_runtime.rs:1334`).

A stranger on a transport that proved no key can register under another peer's name. Because `verified_peer_key()` is `None`, the session is booked under the designator the peer ASSERTED (`book_key = peer.clone()`), and `peer_key` reads that asserted designator as the peer identity; the registry then treats the stranger and the honest peer whose designator it copied as the same peer, so by the crossed-hello rule the honest peer's session is aborted (`admit` returns it as a loser and the caller `abort()`s it). Reachability: `op:start-session` over `tcp-testing-only`/`websocket` with `acceptable-location.designator` set to the victim's designator. This is a stranger doing something a stranger is not meant to do — acting under another peer's name.

Non-adversary control, and she REACHES the function as its governed subject rather than acting against it: the honest validator's own proposal path runs the attestation guard — the decision (nothing_to_finalize / new_state_transition / quorum_reachable / cadence_due) that decides whether this node may emit the attestation finality needs — and only then signs a block. This is the executable surface the statement constrains, so the control is non-vacuous.

The block the honest validator signs carries a `fringe` it derived itself through the single liveness rule (`calculate_finalization` = live_weight_set partition + whole-bonded-map quorum); a peer validating that block re-derives the same fringe from its justifications before the state hash is accepted, so Alice's honest block is the input both halves of the statement (safety via the committed fringe, liveness via the attestation) run on.

Byzantine reachability, deviation 1 — equivowithholdsign two blocks at one height: the node ships an injection that broadcasts an equally-signed twin of every block it creates, producing two distinct signed blocks at one (sender, seq_num). The twin is reachable and lands on the H-1 equivocation gate on insert.

Byzantine reachability, deviation 2 — withhold / selectively delay: a bonded validator that stops producing is exactly the input the live weight set is written for (`is_some_and` over heights behind the tip, retiring a sender past LIVENESS_WINDOW); the same rule feeds the finalizer's partition and the proposer's guard, so Oscar's silence/delay reaches the function.

Byzantine reachability, deviation 3 — lie inside the protocol: a wire block carrying a false block_number / seq_num / state hash is accepted by ingress and is checked only by a receiving peer's block_summary (sequence_number then block_number) before insert, so a false block reaches the function's validation gate.

Byzantine reachability, deviation 4 — attest a lie: the node's finality-attestation endpoint signs `blake2b256(tag||nonce||block_hash)` with its own identity for any block hash it holds, so a validator can sign 'I finalised X' for a block it never finalised — a reachable, attributable in-protocol lie that only the signature-to-key binding constrains.

Production visibility is durable (`latest_block_number` reads the DAG representation, node/src/api/block_api.rs / block_api_impl.rs:335) — so a restart erases exactly the fields the surface exists to expose: after a restart that follows a halt, /api/status reads autoproposeTimerHalted=false, finalityStallEpisodes=0, resetMarker=null, and nothing distinguishes 'never faulted' from 'faulted, then the operator restarted'. Reachability requires only the operator's normal privilege (own the process and restart it — SIGTERM/redeploy), which is the documented and only cure for the halt ('nothing restarts it but the process', ProposerHealth.autopropose_timer_halted doc).

Names the recovery anchor directly when the net has no finality left. No node can attest a meet, so RECONCILE_ANCHOR becomes the block the restore acts on; the tool prints 'This is **your** root, not a computed meet: this tool has verified that <master> holds the block and nothing else about it — not that stake finalised it, not that any other node agrees.' A choice the rule cannot distinguish from a derivation (the census row 'operator error during recovery'; falsifier = a reconciliation that selects a winner by preference rather than by the rule).

Chooses the surviving node and copies its chain state onto every joiner with NO re-verification (--restore-from-master). The tool's own comment says it 'copies the survivor's chain state onto each joiner, so what the joiners agree about afterwards is the *survivor's view*, including the blocks above the agreed anchor that only it accepted. The operator is asserting a winner'. A faulty --master therefore installs that node's diverged view on the whole net — an operator fault that reaches the advance/restore function end to end.

Sets the running node's own restore/advance switches at launch: --self-reset (on a spent divergence budget, rewind the DAG to the last finalised block, purge the bodies above it, move CURRENT_ROOT, re-sync from a bootstrap) and --sync-anchor (restore a node with no chain to a named block). Both are refused at config load when there is no bootstrap or the node is standalone — so the operator's switch, not the node, decides whether a restore is even attempted.

blocked.why: The advance/restore decision consumes only two things, neither of which this persona can write. (1) The operator's own argv/env knobs — RECONCILE_ANCHOR, --master, --self-reset, --sync-anchor (tools/reconcile-network.sh:615; node/src/configuration/commandline/options.rs:660,686). The persona reads env and argv, but reading is knowledge, not actuation — it is explicitly 'NOT the operator', so it cannot set them. (2) The node's own cryptographic rules (hash preimage + signature), re-derived locally; nothing Root can read feeds the restore as a writable input. The boot-side restore guard's trigger is the reset *marker*, a WRITE into the dagstorage DB (casper/src/engine/reset.rs:117 read_reset_marker; block-storage/src/dag/dag_storage.rs:60 RESET_MARKER_KEY; casper/src/storage.rs:24 RESET_MARKER_DB), and the capability model grants this persona only *read* of the data directory, not write. Its single write capability — swapping the image or the release artefact — lands on other study nodes' surfaces: N5 (key lifecycle), N6 (host/container containment), N7 (release provenance). That includes the reconcile tool's verifier, which is resolved from that very artefact (tools/reconcile-network.sh:436-446 rnode_bin: $RECONCILE_RNODE, PATH, ./target/{release,debug}/rnode), so subverting it is an N7 finding and is not a reachability fact for N11's resume/restore property. N11's own census rows — 'silence of a quorum' (stop two of four, restore both) and 'operator error during recovery' — are controlled by the operator and by validator availability, neither of which Root can actuate: it cannot set the anchor, cannot stop/return a validator, and cannot write the reset marker. Barrier stands.

Reachable, but the property holds: every unauthenticated surface Mallory can inject on bounds its input, and every inherently superlinear algorithm in the node is capped, budgeted, or fixed, so no reachable action's cost grows faster than linearly in Mallory's input. Reachability (not the barrier): the transport accepts ANY self-signed P-256 client cert -- NodeIdClientVerifier::verify_client_cert checks only current validity and a well-formed key, with no trust chain -- so comm/src/transport/hostname_trust_manager.rs:143-158 lets Mallory connect as its own node id; the deploy gRPC/HTTP, public read and Kademlia surfaces are unauthenticated (the C115 sender-binding only pins the claimed id to the cert). The barrier is the layered bounds: (1) inbound transport is size- and concurrency-bounded -- per-stream max_stream_message_size enforced while draining plus an aggregate byte budget (comm/src/transport/grpc_transport_receiver.rs:470-493), MAX_STREAM_CHUNKS=100000 (:320), MAX_CONCURRENT_DISPATCH/STREAMS/BLOBS + a 10s handshake timeout under a semaphore (:199-212,:288); (2) decompression is rejected before allocating past the cap (comm/src/transport/stream_handler.rs:185); (3) connection/lookup work is bounded -- MAX_CONNECTIONS=1024 with a dial budget (comm/src/rp/connect.rs:20,165), a Kademlia token-bucket rate limit (comm/src/discovery/grpc_kademlia_rpc_server.rs:48) and an O(1)-per-call limiter (shared/src/rate_limiter.rs:33); (4) deploy flooding is O(1) amortized per deploy and capped -- MAX_POOLED_DEPLOYS=10000 with an O(1) count() gate and no pool scan in add_deploy (casper/src/dag.rs:32,1046); (5) block processing is capped -- <=255 deploys and MAX_BLOCK_PHLO=2.55e10 (casper/src/validate.rs:648,667); (6) every superlinear algorithm is fixed or budgeted -- nested-tuple parser exponential closed (rholang/src/parser.rs:2080, fix 500d35e3d), par_set/par_map dedup Theta(N^2)->Theta(N log N) (models/src/sorter.rs:843,860), diff_cost charges the product (rholang/src/accounting.rs:111), the four cubic rho:gov:* folds capped at MAX_GOV_UNIVERSE=512 and charged quadratically (rholang/src/system_processes.rs:1273, rholang/src/accounting.rs:124), RSpace subset matching capped (rholang/src/matcher/par_spatial_matcher_utils.rs:93,176), and the exponential merge search bounded by SearchBudget::NODE (sdk/src/dag/merging.rs:280). The residual superlinear paths that remain (gov cubic, merge search) are CAPPED, so aggregate cost over a flood is linear; none is reachable uncapped by Mallory.

Passive reader: she can read the plaintext deploy (40401) and blocks, but issuing a send or a read-query is an active act she cannot perform. Reading the deploy plaintext buys her nothing anyway: on the consensus path the fresh names are NOT a function of (deployer,timestamp) — the deploy's RNG is the block seed (rholang/src/reduce.rs:2376 draws from the deploy rand; casper/src/runtime_manager.rs:712-714 sets that rand = block_seed.split_byte(i).split_byte(1); casper/src/block_random_seed.rs:123-138 derives the seed from shard_id/block_number/sender/pre_state_hash). And even a predicted name cannot be used: no Rholang term can construct a GPrivate (rholang/src/system_processes.rs:262-264). Barrier: passive capability + the construction barrier.

Active on unauthenticated surfaces, and he CAN build a Par carrying an arbitrary GPrivate at the API edge (node/src/api/rho_expr.rs:336 RhoName::apply_bytes(hex)). But that Par only reaches the two READ APIs — getDataAtPar and listenForDataAtName (node/src/api/web_api_impl.rs:1321,1334) — which read store data; it never reaches evaluation, because a deploy's term is Rholang source (models/src/casper/protocol/casper_message.rs:53 term: String) and no Rholang term constructs a GPrivate (rholang/src/system_processes.rs:262-264, pinned by the test at rholang/src/system_processes.rs:4386). So Mallory can read at a name (a disclosure, N3's property) but cannot forge a send. Pre-seal he cannot even predict the name (block seed). Barrier: the eval path is source-only + the construction barrier.

The one actor who can PREDICT the seed before execution: as proposer he computes the block rand from public fields (shard_id, block_num, his own pk, pre_state_hash) before running any deploy (casper/src/blocks/proposer/block_creator.rs:93-99), and each deploy's first fresh name is that seed split by position then by index (casper/src/runtime_manager.rs:712-714 -> rholang/src/reduce.rs:2376). But prediction confers no forge: his own deploy cannot construct the victim's GPrivate (rholang/src/system_processes.rs:262-264), a private name is never placed in the store so it cannot be received, and he executes the whole block atomically anyway. Barrier: prediction without the construction capability — the property is held by construction, not by secrecy.

Host / supply-chain intruder (reads the data dir and key files, swaps the image). The consensus names carry no host secret to capture: the seed is public block data (casper/src/block_random_seed.rs:123-138), so reading the host yields nothing a public reader lacks. The OS CSPRNG (crypto/src/hash/blake2b512_random.rs:111-114, rand::rng()) is used only on the non-consensus explore/preview path (node/src/web/transaction.rs:306 default_random), which forges no consensus name. Barrier: no secret in this node's derivation for Root to steal; the entropy substrate is the block itself, not the host.

The trusted operator is a fault source, not an adversary, and is declared out of model (In-model? = outside; preregistration.md §2). The only operator-controlled input is shard_id — public genesis config — used to derive the genesis fixed names (casper/src/block_random_seed.rs:140+ split_random_number_from_genesis), which a public reader recomputes identically. Barrier: out of model / no adversary gain.

Honest validator — the non-adversary control. Mechanically she recomputes the block seed every replay (the replay splits exactly as the play path does, casper/src/runtime_replay.rs:243,293,351), so she could compute the same names Oscar can; but she is the control and, like every actor, cannot construct a GPrivate to send on one (rholang/src/system_processes.rs:262-264). Barrier: control persona + the construction barrier.

Honest client / deployer / public reader — the control. He submits source-only deploys (models/src/casper/protocol/casper_message.rs:53) and reads chain state, but cannot construct a name (rholang/src/system_processes.rs:262-264) and cannot predict one pre-seal (the seed needs the sealed pre_state_hash, casper/src/block_random_seed.rs:123-138). Barrier: control persona + the construction barrier.

reached.fact: As a validator, Oscar sets the `timestamp` field of every block he signs, and the node neither validates nor bounds it. The node adopts that value as the block's time and republishes it verbatim to every Rholang contract in the block through `rho:block:data` (BlockData::from_block copies block.timestamp; the handler replies it as an integer) — so the time the node reports is a single validator's choice, unvalidated (validate.rs's block_summary and the whole validation path contain no timestamp check). The same remote value is then compared against the node's OWN wall clock on the receiver to decide whether to treat the validator's block as a live round worth attesting (attest_is_live(block.timestamp, now)); that gate is a fixed 15 s constant and one-sided (a future stamp is treated as live, a past one dropped), and uses saturating_sub so an absurd timestamp cannot crash it. Reachability fact: Oscar's chosen timestamp enters the node's observable time output and its attestation gate. Boundary: the timestamp is inside the content-addressed block hash, so Oscar can only set it on blocks he signs, not alter another validator's; and because the timestamp is pinned in the header and no validation reads it, a validator cannot be made to reject its own block on a time basis (the node's 'bounded' half holds for consensus).
reached.citation: rholang/src/system_processes.rs:243 (BlockData::from_block: `timestamp: block.timestamp`) -> rholang/src/system_processes.rs:1438 (get_block_data replies `RhoNumber::apply(timestamp)`); node/src/runtime/node_runtime.rs:1822 (`if !attest_is_live(block.timestamp, now)`), with the bound at node/src/runtime/node_runtime.rs:3036-3043 (ATTEST_MAX_BLOCK_AGE_MS = ROUND_STALL_ESCAPE = 15 s; `now_ms.saturating_sub(block_ms) <= ATTEST_MAX_BLOCK_AGE_MS`); proposer origin casper/src/blocks/proposer/block_creator.rs:82 (`let block_timestamp = current_millis()`)

findings.persona: Eve
findings.deviation: The Kademlia discovery server is served with NO inbound decode cap, so it accepts messages up to tonic's default (4 MiB) — 16x the operator's configured protocol-server.grpc-max-recv-message-size (256 KiB, defaults.conf:47) that the peer transport honours. A peer's discovery message is therefore not bounded in size as configured: an authenticated peer can force a 4 MiB Ping/Lookup decode (allocation, plus a peer-chosen host string into is_local_address_resolved/DNS) where the operator believes 256 KiB is in force. This is the exact C113 class ('the server never set the cap') one service over from where it was fixed. Eve's vantage: she reads no byte of the mTLS transport, so this is read from source; the trigger needs a certificate-bearing peer (in the network-adversary model).
findings.reachFact: comm/src/discovery/grpc_kademlia_rpc_server.rs:174 (`.add_service(KademliaRpcServiceServer::new(service))` — no `.max_decoding_message_size(...)`), contrasted with comm/src/transport/grpc_transport_receiver.rs:632
findings.falsifier: owed: a test that opens the Kademlia service and sends a `Lookup` whose encoded size exceeds protocol-server.grpc-max-recv-message-size, asserting the call is refused. No such test exists; the transport's twin is pinned only for the transport (grpc_transport_receiver.rs max_recv cap).

findings.persona: Eve
findings.deviation: Authentication covers only the PART of a peer message that carries a well-formed header. On the unary path the wrong-network rejection is inside `if let Some(header)` (line 386) and the sender-identity binding is inside `if let Ok(sender) = protocol_helper::sender(&protocol)` (line 410) — and sender() errors with HeaderNotAvailable/SenderNotAvailable when the header or its sender field is absent — so a Protocol with no header (or a sender-less header) is dispatched with NEITHER the network-id check NOR the sender binding. The stream breaker (line 508) likewise wraps both checks in `if let Some(header)`, skipping SenderNotVerified when the reassembled header is absent. Downstream routing keys on the sender, so a peer can reach the dispatch with an unproven/absent sender identity. Requires an authenticated connection to deliver it (the identity-binding is the app-layer half the mTLS does not supply), in the network-adversary model.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/transport/grpc_transport_receiver.rs:410 (with the companion conditionals at :386 and :508)
findings.falsifier: owed: a test that sends a headerless Protocol (or a header with no sender) over an authenticated connection and asserts permission_denied; none exists — the for_test seam pins other guards but not this.

findings.persona: Eve
findings.deviation: A peer's LookupResponse is acted on in the REVERSE direction — the node dials a target the peer named. The discovery client collapses the response's nodes into peers with NO local-address filter (`.nodes.iter().filter_map(|n| to_peer_node(n).ok())`), discover() records them into the routing table unfiltered (store.update_last_seen), and find_and_connect→connect (comm/src/rp/connect.rs) dials each by host:port with no loopback guard. The loopback/link-local/unspecified guard exists ONLY on the inbound sender (grpc_kademlia_rpc_server.rs:94/126), so a malicious authenticated peer answering a Lookup with a Node whose host is 127.0.0.1 (or a name resolving to loopback) makes the victim node connect to its own loopback services — SSRF steered by a peer's message. The peer must be an authenticated node (cert), i.e. in the network-adversary model.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/discovery/grpc_kademlia_rpc.rs:123 (the unfiltered `.filter_map(|n| to_peer_node(n).ok())`), with the unfiltered record at comm/src/discovery/kademlia_node_discovery.rs:19
findings.falsifier: owed: a test in which a LookupResponse names host 127.0.0.1 and the node is asserted not to record/dial it. No such test exists (the SSRF tests cover only the inbound sender path).

findings.persona: Mallory
findings.deviation: There is no rate bound on the inbound transport surface; 'rate' is realised only as in-flight CONCURRENCY, and the permit is released the instant a dispatch/stream completes, so an anonymous peer's sustained messages-per-second is unbounded (bounded above only by 1024 outstanding). The node's own Kademlia surface has a real token bucket; the transport has none.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/transport/grpc_transport_receiver.rs:427 (dispatch_slots.try_acquire_owned, permit moved into the spawned task and released at :433-435) and :453 (stream_slots); the receiver imports no rate limiter — the workspace's only RateLimiter (shared/src/rate_limiter.rs) is wired solely into the Kademlia service (comm/src/discovery/grpc_kademlia_rpc_server.rs:68).
findings.falsifier: owed: measure admitted messages/second from one anonymous peer over a fixed window; because the semaphore returns a permit on completion (grpc_transport_receiver.rs:433), a fast peer exceeds any per-second figure a rate bound would set.

findings.persona: Mallory
findings.deviation: The Kademlia rate bound is one GLOBAL token bucket shared by every peer, so one anonymous peer spending it reduces every other peer's allowance to zero — the rate a victim actually receives is far less than the configured 100/s, and discovery can be withheld from the whole honest network by a single caller.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/discovery/grpc_kademlia_rpc_server.rs:68 (a single RateLimiter::new(100) stored in the server struct), :76 and :112 (allow() with no key/peer/connection dimension); shared/src/rate_limiter.rs holds one (tokens, Instant) state behind one Mutex, with no per-caller map.
findings.falsifier: client A spends the bucket, then a single ping from client B returns Status::resource_exhausted — the present test (grpc_kademlia_rpc_server.rs:529) only ever exercises one caller.

findings.persona: Mallory
findings.deviation: A rate/concurrency rejection is reported to the sender as a SIZE error: ResourceExhausted (dispatch/stream/blob slot exhausted) maps to CommError::MessageTooLarge, so 'the bound refused you' is indistinguishable from 'your message was too big' — an operator sees a size problem that is really a saturation of a rate-adjacent bound.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/transport/grpc_transport.rs:39 (Code::ResourceExhausted => CommError::MessageTooLarge); the receiver returns ResourceExhausted for a full dispatch queue (grpc_transport_receiver.rs:429), stream slots (:455) and decompressed blob slots (:537).

findings.persona: Mallory
findings.deviation: A heartbeat does MORE than signal liveness: it moves the sender to the END of the bounded connection table, so a heartbeating peer escapes the oldest-first eviction that a handshake-only peer suffers. An anonymous peer can heartbeat its 1024 fresh ids to entrench them and evict honest peers from a full table.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/rp/handle_messages.rs:150-153 (Heartbeat => refresh_conn), comm/src/rp/connect.rs:68-80 (refresh_conn moves the matched id to the end) together with comm/src/rp/connect.rs:50-52 (over MAX_CONNECTIONS=1024 the FRONT/oldest entries are drained).
findings.falsifier: fill the table with MAX_CONNECTIONS peers, heartbeat one, add a new peer, and assert the heartbeated peer survives the eviction while an un-heartbeated one (closer to the front) is dropped.

findings.persona: Mallory
findings.deviation: The Kademlia rate token is spent BEFORE the network-id and identity checks, so an anonymous peer can drain the shared bucket with wrong-network or spoofed-sender requests the node rejects anyway — the bound is consumed on work that is discarded, amplifying the DoS in the LESS finding.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/discovery/grpc_kademlia_rpc_server.rs:76 and :112 (rate_limiter.allow()) precede :88 and :121 (network-id check) and :95 and :127 (sender_not_proven).
findings.falsifier: send 100 wrong-network pings, then an honest lookup from another peer returns Status::resource_exhausted — the bucket was spent on requests refused at :88/:121.

findings.persona: Oscar — a Byzantine consensus participant: at most one malicious validator (under a third of the stake), holding a valid transport certificate, able to sign two blocks at a height, withhold, selectively delay, and lie inside the protocol.
findings.deviation: The streamed path's sender/network binding runs LATE — after the whole stream has been received and metered. The circuit breaker that compares the stream header's sender to the certificate-proven id, and the network-id check, both live inside `collect`, which is called AFTER the drain loop has consumed every chunk and charged the aggregate budget. So a peer whose header will fail the binding still forces the node to buffer, size-check and budget-charge the entire stream first, then be refused — the authentication decision is ordered after the resource spend it should precede.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/transport/grpc_transport_receiver.rs:507-520 — the breaker (`SenderNotVerified` at :513, `WrongNetworkId` at :510) is invoked from `stream_handler::collect` at :522, which runs after the drain loop at :470-494 has already charged `charge_stream_budget` (:480). The header arrives as the first chunk but is not examined until after the drain.
findings.falsifier: Send a stream whose header `sender` != the cert id; measure that the node has drained and charged the whole stream before rejecting it. Fires (closes) if the binding is checked at the first (header) chunk, before the drain loop runs.

findings.persona: Alice — honest bonded validator (non-adversary control): her transport heartbeat/handshake/packet and her discovery ping/lookup genuinely traverse N1 on 40400/40404, admitted under her certificate-proven id; she deviates nothing, so every finding below is a deviation of the node's own mechanism that an authenticated in-model peer (a class Alice's reachability demonstrates) can reach — not something Alice does.

An authenticated peer whose stream header sender differs from its certificate still makes the node buffer up to the per-stream cap, charge the aggregate budget and hold a slot before rejection. The unary path checks first; this path checks last.
findings.reachFact: comm/src/transport/grpc_transport_receiver.rs:453 (stream_slots permit acquired first) and :470-494 (chunks drained and buffered) versus :522 (`stream_handler::collect(...)` runs the breaker defined at :507-520, whose sender check is at :512); the identity decision is made after the resource is committed.
